title: Hell
hookLine: traditions teach eternal separation; some hold that the lost cease to be; some hope all may be saved

cards: Near Jerusalem lies a valley. The Bible calls it the valley of the son of Hinnom, and Jeremiah says a terrible thing was done there: children burned in the fire, something God says he never commanded.
When Jesus warns about hell in Matthew, the Greek word is Gehenna, and readers trace it to that valley's name. On that reading, a real place of horror became the name for final loss.
It's a hard subject, and the churches hold it in more than one way.

teach.b: Start with what Jesus says, because he says it seriously. In Matthew, after the sheep and the goats are separated: "these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal."

And elsewhere he says to fear the one "which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell." Catholic and Orthodox teaching, and the classic Protestant confessions, hold that hell is real and lasting: separation from God.
Catholic teaching describes it as a person's own final choice to shut God out, not God's wish.
Some Christians read that other line, destroy both soul and body, and hold that the lost finally cease to be. The fire, they say, is final, not endless.

And some Christians, including some Orthodox writers, hope that God's love may in the end reach everyone. They lean on Paul, who says God "will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth."
They hold it as a hope, not a promise. These readings disagree, and the disagreement matters. But they share two things.
Each takes evil and its cost seriously. And each reads the same verse about God's heart.

teach.h: A HOPE THAT ALL BE SAVED.
teach.b: Peter writes that the Lord is "not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance."

teach.h: NOT WILLING THAT ANY SHOULD PERISH.
teach.b: On that verse, no one's loss is what God wants. An old hymn puts it in a line: "There's a wideness in God's mercy."

how: Christians meet the teaching on hell in the Gospels' warnings and in the creeds' judgment of the living and the dead; Catholic and Orthodox teaching and the classic Protestant confessions hold it as real and lasting separation from God, while some Christians hold other views.

games.q: someone asks you: "does God want anyone lost?" which line from today answers most directly?
games.why: Peter: the Lord is "not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance." the churches read the warnings differently, and each reads this verse too.

practice: Start close, with the people in your home and the people you'll see today, then widen to your street, your city, people you'll never meet.
Then the hard ones, someone who hurt you, someone whose choices you can't understand, without arguing over whether they deserve it.
If you pray, bring them before God, the way Paul asks prayers to be made for all; if you don't, wish each one well, as widely as you can reach.

wordCard.voice: Hell. In the Gospels, Gehenna: a word readers trace to a valley's name, used for final loss. Churches read it as lasting separation, as an end, or alongside a hope that all be saved.

orig.note: Greek: Gehenna, the word for hell in Jesus's warnings in Matthew, traced by readers to the name of the valley of Hinnom.

carryVoice: Your line: his mercy is wide. Peter's verse, read by every view. See you tomorrow.
